solution.concept_anchor: On-balance-sheet lending vs. BC-based credit facilitation distinction

statement_analysis.statement: A payments bank cannot extend loans, credit cards, or advances of any kind directly to its customers, as these activities constitute on-balance-sheet credit extension prohibited under its license.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the most fundamental restriction under the payments bank licensing framework. All forms of direct credit — personal loans, business loans, credit cards, mortgages — are prohibited because they expose the payments bank's balance sheet to credit risk.

statement_analysis.statement: Because payments banks are prohibited from lending, they are also barred from participating in any activity that results in credit reaching their customers, including acting as agents or intermediaries for commercial banks.
statement_analysis.reason: Payments banks can act as Business Correspondents of commercial banks, which involves facilitating loan origination and disbursement on behalf of the commercial bank. This is a permitted fee-based activity that does not involve the payments bank extending credit from its own balance sheet.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) suggests both statements are correct, which attracts students who read Statement 2 as a logical extension of Statement 1 — 'if you can't lend, you can't help others lend.' This reversed-causation reasoning ignores the principal/agent distinction.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Direct lending in any form is prohibited for payments banks — this is unambiguously correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The prohibition is on direct, on-balance-sheet credit extension. Acting as a BC is an off-balance-sheet, fee-based service explicitly permitted by RBI guidelines — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 is correct; Statement 2 is incorrect — select option (c).
Wait — re-check: correct answer should be (c) per the option structure: Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap in Statement 2 builds a logically seductive chain: 'payments banks cannot lend → therefore they cannot facilitate lending in any form.' This causal extension is false. The legal distinction is between principal liability (on-balance-sheet lending — prohibited) and agent-based facilitation (BC role — permitted). The BC earns a fee but does not bear credit risk. Students who apply the lending prohibition broadly without understanding this principal/agent distinction will incorrectly validate Statement 2.
solution.final_explanation:
The lending prohibition and the BC role represent two legally distinct activities that must not be conflated.

• Statement 1 — Correct: All forms of direct credit extension — personal loans, business loans, consumer credit, mortgages, credit cards — are prohibited for payments banks. The prohibition covers any on-balance-sheet credit exposure to customers.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The BC model is explicitly carved out as a permitted activity. A payments bank acting as a BC for a commercial bank collects loan applications, verifies customer information, and facilitates disbursement — but the credit decision, credit risk, and balance sheet exposure all rest with the commercial bank. The payments bank earns a transaction fee and incurs no credit risk. RBI guidelines explicitly permit this arrangement.

Value Addition:
• The BC-based credit facilitation model is central to last-mile financial inclusion — bringing formal credit to customers who cannot access commercial bank branches.
• Fee income from BC services is one of the few diversified revenue streams for payments banks given their restricted product menu.
• The distinction between being a lender (principal) and a distributor (agent) is fundamental in financial regulatory law and appears across insurance, securities, and banking frameworks.

solution.final_explanation:
The Paytm Payments Bank case illustrates active regulatory enforcement and the basis of RBI's supervisory authority.

Assertion (A): Correct. In early 2024, RBI directed Paytm Payments Bank to stop accepting deposits and top-ups, citing persistent KYC violations, inadequate customer due diligence, and data-sharing arrangements with parent entity One97 Communications. This was a formal supervisory action with significant business consequences.

Reason (R): Correct. Payments banks are licensed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Under this statute, RBI is empowered to issue directives, conduct inspections, impose restrictions, and cancel licenses — comprehensive supervisory authority that applies to all licensed banks including differentiated entities.

Causal relationship: Present and direct. RBI's action against Paytm Payments Bank was a specific exercise of the supervisory powers vested in it by the Banking Regulation Act. The Reason directly explains the institutional basis for the action described in the Assertion.

Option (a) is correct.

Value Addition:
• RBI's SPARC (Supervisory Programme for Assessment of Risk and Capital) framework is the structured methodology through which it monitors payments banks.
• 'Fit and proper' criteria for bank management are enforced by RBI under Section 35B of the Banking Regulation Act.
• Data governance — ensuring that regulated banks do not share customer data with promoter entities — is an emerging regulatory priority globally and in India.

solution.concept_anchor: Payments Banks regulatory parameters — correct attribution of figures

statement_analysis.statement: The minimum paid-up equity capital for a payments bank is Rs. 100 crore, while for a Small Finance Bank it is Rs. 200 crore.
statement_analysis.reason: These figures are correctly attributed: Rs. 100 crore for payments banks and Rs. 200 crore for Small Finance Banks — the two primary differentiated bank categories.

statement_analysis.statement: The maximum per-customer deposit balance in a payments bank was originally set at Rs. 2 lakh and subsequently revised to Rs. 1 lakh in 2021.
statement_analysis.reason: The revision was in the opposite direction: the limit was originally Rs. 1 lakh and was raised to Rs. 2 lakh in 2021. The statement reverses the chronological sequence.

statement_analysis.statement: Payments banks must maintain a minimum CRAR of 15%, while scheduled commercial banks are required to maintain a minimum of approximately 10.875% under Basel III norms.
statement_analysis.reason: The 15% CRAR for payments banks and approximately 10.875% for commercial banks (Tier 1 + Tier 2 under RBI's Basel III implementation) are correctly stated.

statement_analysis.statement: The promoter of a payments bank must hold a minimum of 40% equity for the first five years, after which the holding can be diluted as per the bank's needs.
statement_analysis.reason: RBI requires the promoter to maintain at least 40% paid-up equity for the first five years — a lock-in ensuring committed promoter involvement. After the lock-in, dilution is possible subject to RBI's approval and guidelines.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) suggesting 'only three' is correct is a strong distractor for students who correctly identify Statement 2 as wrong but then doubt one of the other statements due to uncertainty about CRAR figures or promoter lock-in nuances.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Rs. 100 cr (payments banks) vs Rs. 200 cr (SFBs) — correctly stated — Correct.
Statement 2: The deposit limit went from Rs. 1 lakh → Rs. 2 lakh in 2021; the statement reverses the direction — Incorrect.
Statement 3: 15% CRAR for payments banks vs ~10.875% for commercial banks — correctly stated — Correct.
Statement 4: 40% promoter lock-in for first 5 years — correctly stated — Correct.
Three statements (1, 3, 4) are correct — select option (a): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses the reversed-causation variant of the temporal-swap trap — it correctly states both figures (Rs. 1 lakh and Rs. 2 lakh) but reverses their chronological order, claiming Rs. 2 lakh was the original and Rs. 1 lakh was the revision. Students who know both figures exist but have not precisely tracked which came first will find Statement 2 ambiguous, potentially accepting it as correct. The key fact: Rs. 1 lakh was the original 2015 limit; Rs. 2 lakh is the 2021 revision.
solution.final_explanation:
Precise factual accuracy — including correct direction of regulatory changes — is what separates precise from approximate knowledge.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The minimum paid-up equity capital differential between payments banks (Rs. 100 cr) and SFBs (Rs. 200 cr) is correctly attributed — a classic comparative fact.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The revision sequence is reversed. At inception (2015), the deposit ceiling was Rs. 1 lakh. RBI increased it to Rs. 2 lakh in 2021 to make payments banks more competitive and useful for their target customers. Stating the original was Rs. 2 lakh is factually wrong.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Payments banks are subject to a 15% minimum CRAR — higher than commercial banks' ~10.875% minimum under RBI's Basel III-aligned guidelines, reflecting heightened prudential expectations for new institutions.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The 40% promoter lock-in for five years is an established condition designed to prevent short-term speculative interest in banking licenses and ensure skin-in-the-game commitment.

Value Addition:
• Post the 5-year lock-in, promoter dilution follows RBI's guidelines on shareholding patterns — promoter holding must still meet minimum thresholds for continued control.
• The capital differential between payments banks and SFBs is deliberate: SFBs take on credit risk (lending), requiring a larger capital buffer.
• RBI's CRAR requirements are reviewed periodically in line with evolving Basel norms and macroprudential assessments.

solution.concept_anchor: IMPS/NEFT/RTGS access for payments banks — RTGS is high-value, not micro-remittance
solution.strong_distractor: b — NEFT is a large-batch, deferred settlement system and some students may associate it with commercial bank operations not accessible to payments banks, making it seem like the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Check (a): IMPS — Immediate Payment Service — is available to payments banks through NPCI membership, enabling real-time domestic Person-to-Person remittances — a core permitted service.
Check (b): NEFT — National Electronic Funds Transfer — is accessible to payments banks for fund transfers, consistent with their domestic remittance mandate.
Check (c): AePS — Aadhaar-enabled Payment System — is a primary channel for payments banks to serve rural customers with biometric-based transactions.

Check (d): RTGS — Real Time Gross Settlement — is designed for high-value interbank settlements (minimum Rs. 2 lakh per transaction). While payments bank customers may send RTGS through the banking system, it is structurally misaligned with the micro-remittance and low-value transaction profile of payments bank customers. Among these four systems, RTGS is the least naturally aligned with the payments bank use case.
RTGS is the odd one out — select (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges all four payment systems as equally 'accessible' to payments banks without distinguishing their use-case fit. RTGS requires a minimum transaction value of Rs. 2 lakh — the same as the entire deposit ceiling for payments bank customers. This structural mismatch means RTGS is conceptually incompatible with the payments bank model, even if technically accessible through interbank clearing. Students who view all four as equivalent payment rails will not notice this operational misalignment.
solution.final_explanation:
Payment systems accessible to payments banks vary in their alignment with the payments bank use case.

• Option (a) — IMPS: Belongs to the group. Immediate Payment Service enables 24x7 real-time fund transfers with no minimum amount floor — perfectly suited for small, time-sensitive remittances by migrant workers, the core payments bank customer.
• Option (b) — NEFT: Belongs to the group. National Electronic Funds Transfer, now operating on a continuous settlement basis (not batched), enables low-value domestic remittances accessible through payments bank accounts.
• Option (c) — AePS: Belongs to the group. The Aadhaar-enabled Payment System is specifically designed for biometric-based transactions in low-connectivity rural areas — a defining delivery channel for payments banks like IPPB.
• Option (d) — RTGS: The odd one out. Real Time Gross Settlement is designed for high-value interbank fund transfers with a minimum threshold of Rs. 2 lakh per transaction. This equals the entire per-customer deposit ceiling in payments banks, making RTGS structurally misaligned with the low-value, micro-remittance profile of payments bank customers.

Value Addition:
• NEFT and RTGS are operated by RBI; IMPS and AePS are operated by NPCI.
• From December 2019, NEFT became available 24x7 — removing its earlier batch-processing limitation.
• Payments banks primarily use IMPS and UPI for customer-facing remittances due to real-time settlement and no minimum value restrictions.

solution.concept_anchor: Dual regulatory interface — payments banks as Corporate Agents for insurance

statement_analysis.statement: When a payments bank acts as a Corporate Agent for insurance products, it is regulated simultaneously by both the Reserve Bank of India (for banking operations) and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) for its insurance distribution activities.
statement_analysis.reason: Payments banks acting as Corporate Agents for insurance are subject to IRDAI's corporate agent regulations in addition to RBI's banking regulations — creating a genuine dual-regulator interface for the distribution activity.

statement_analysis.statement: Payments banks are permitted to underwrite insurance policies on their own balance sheet, provided they obtain a separate registration from IRDAI as an insurance company.
statement_analysis.reason: Payments banks can only distribute insurance products as agents (Corporate Agents) — they cannot underwrite policies. Underwriting requires a full insurance license under the Insurance Act, 1938, which is a wholly separate regulatory framework incompatible with the payments bank model.

statement_analysis.statement: The cross-selling of mutual fund products, insurance policies, and NPS subscriptions by payments banks is best understood as a business model diversification strategy to compensate for the absence of net interest margin income.
statement_analysis.reason: Since payments banks cannot earn NIM (no lending), fee-based income from third-party product distribution — mutual funds, insurance, NPS — is a primary business model diversification strategy. This is widely recognised in RBI's framework and policy discussions.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) suggesting only Statement 1 is NOT correct attracts students who find the dual-regulator interface claim in Statement 1 difficult to believe — it sounds complex and therefore 'possibly wrong.'
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The dual-regulator interface for Corporate Agent insurance distribution is factually established — Statement 1 is correct, so it is NOT the answer to 'not correct'.
Evaluate Statement 2: Payments banks cannot underwrite insurance; only distribution as an agent is permitted — Statement 2 IS incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Third-party distribution as NIM-compensation strategy is correctly characterised — Statement 3 is correct, not the answer to 'not correct'.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a plausible fabrication: it sounds administratively possible that a bank could get separate IRDAI registration to underwrite insurance, especially given that some banking conglomerates do have insurance subsidiaries. The key distinction is that payments banks specifically cannot set up subsidiaries (including insurance companies), and the Corporate Agent role is a distribution — not underwriting — relationship. The phrase 'on their own balance sheet' is the key error, as underwriting means bearing insurance risk directly.
solution.final_explanation:
The revenue model diversification of payments banks through third-party product distribution involves specific permitted and prohibited activities.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The dual-regulator interface is a real feature of payments bank operations when they act as Corporate Agents. RBI governs their banking license; IRDAI governs their insurance distribution compliance. This creates parallel compliance obligations under two regulatory frameworks.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Payments banks can only distribute insurance as Corporate Agents — they earn commissions but bear no insurance risk. Underwriting insurance (bearing the actuarial risk of claims) requires a full-fledged insurance company license under the Insurance Act, 1938, which payments banks cannot obtain given the subsidiary restriction.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The absence of NIM (since no lending is permitted) makes fee income from third-party distribution a structural necessity, not a choice. Mutual fund distribution (SEBI/AMFI regulated), insurance distribution (IRDAI regulated), and NPS PoP services (PFRDA regulated) constitute the core diversification strategy.

Value Addition:
• A Corporate Agent can represent multiple insurance companies — up to 3 life, 3 general, and 3 health insurers — under IRDAI's 2015 Corporate Agent Regulations.
• PFRDA regulates NPS Points of Presence; payments banks acting as PoPs are subject to PFRDA guidelines alongside RBI regulations.
• The multi-regulator compliance burden is itself a cost and risk factor for payments banks.

solution.concept_anchor: Differentiated bank license — meaning of 'differentiated' in RBI framework
solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Scheduled bank' is a strong distractor because payments banks are listed in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, making them scheduled banks — but this is a different classification from 'differentiated'.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): 'Universal bank' license permits all banking activities with no activity restrictions — the opposite of what payments banks hold.

Eliminate (c): 'Scheduled bank' refers to listing in the Second Schedule of RBI Act — a membership classification, not a licensing type. Payments banks are scheduled banks, but the blank is asking about the type of license.
Eliminate (d): 'Non-banking financial company' is a non-bank entity — payments banks are licensed banks.
Confirm (a): 'Differentiated bank' license means the institution is restricted to specific activities as defined by RBI — precisely the category under which both payments banks and SFBs are licensed.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges 'scheduled bank' status with the licensing type. Payments banks ARE scheduled banks (they appear in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act) but they hold a 'differentiated' bank license — not a 'scheduled bank license' (which is not a license type; it is a membership classification). Students who know payments banks are scheduled banks may conflate this membership status with the type of license they hold, selecting option (c).
solution.final_explanation:
The licensing framework is distinct from the membership classification of banks.

• Option (a) — Correct: 'Differentiated bank' is the license category under which payments banks and small finance banks operate. 'Differentiated' signifies that the bank is licensed to perform only a defined subset of banking activities — in the case of payments banks, focused on payments and deposit services without lending.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: A 'universal bank' license permits the full spectrum of banking activities — loans, deposits, treasury, investment banking, etc. Commercial banks like SBI and HDFC Bank hold universal licenses. Payments banks do not.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: 'Scheduled bank' status refers to a bank's inclusion in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934 — it signals eligibility for RBI's liquidity support and clearing membership. This is a membership classification, not a license type. Payments banks can be (and are) scheduled banks, but their license type is 'differentiated.'
• Option (d) — Incorrect: An NBFC is not a bank at all — it is a non-bank financial company regulated under the RBI Act but without a banking license.

Value Addition:
• RBI introduced the differentiated licensing framework in 2014–15, departing from its earlier policy of issuing only universal bank licenses.
• Both payments banks and small finance banks are 'differentiated banks' — different mandates under the same licensing category.
• Being a scheduled bank gives payments banks access to RTGS, NEFT, and IMPS interbank systems as direct participants.

solution.concept_anchor: Core restrictions matrix — what payments banks can and cannot do

statement_analysis.statement: A payments bank can open savings accounts and current accounts but cannot accept time deposits such as fixed deposits from its customers.
statement_analysis.reason: Payments banks are restricted to demand deposits — savings and current accounts. Time deposits (fixed deposits, recurring deposits) are explicitly prohibited under RBI's licensing guidelines.

statement_analysis.statement: A payments bank can issue debit cards linked to customer savings accounts but cannot issue credit cards to any category of customer.
statement_analysis.reason: Issuing debit cards (which draw on existing deposit balances) is permitted. Credit cards, which extend revolving credit to customers, are a form of unsecured lending and are explicitly prohibited.

statement_analysis.statement: A payments bank can set up subsidiaries to conduct microfinance and small business lending, provided it receives prior approval from the RBI.
statement_analysis.reason: Payments banks are explicitly barred from setting up subsidiaries to undertake NBFC activities, including microfinance or any form of lending. Prior RBI approval does not override this structural prohibition.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) suggesting all three are correct is the strongest distractor because Statement 3 includes 'provided it receives prior approval from RBI' — a qualification that makes the prohibition sound like a waivable condition rather than an absolute restriction.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Demand deposits (savings and current) permitted; time deposits prohibited — correctly stated — Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Debit cards permitted, credit cards prohibited — the distinction tracks the lending prohibition accurately — Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: No subsidiary for NBFC activities is an absolute structural prohibition — prior RBI approval cannot override this foundational restriction — Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct; Statement 3 is incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the scope-extension technique by adding 'provided it receives prior approval from RBI' — a conditionally worded exception that sounds administratively legitimate. Students who know RBI has broad discretionary powers may accept that approval could open the subsidiary route. In fact, the prohibition on NBFC subsidiaries is a structural condition of the payments bank license design, not a default that can be waived by RBI approval. This is a deliberately inserted false escape clause.
solution.final_explanation:
The restrictions on payments banks operate at a structural level and cannot be individually waived through approvals.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Demand deposits (savings and current accounts) represent the only deposit product payments banks can offer. Fixed deposits, recurring deposits, and other time deposits require a deposit commitment beyond the on-demand framework and are prohibited.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Debit cards access existing deposit balances and do not involve credit extension — they are permitted. Credit cards, which extend unsecured credit up to a preset limit, constitute lending and are prohibited in line with the no-lending rule.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The prohibition on NBFC subsidiaries is a foundational structural restriction embedded in the payments bank licensing framework. No provision allows this restriction to be waived through prior RBI approval. This restriction ensures the no-lending mandate is not circumvented through subsidiary structures.

Value Addition:
• The NBFC subsidiary restriction mirrors the policy principle that payments banks should not use indirect routes to achieve what is directly prohibited.
• Prepaid payment instruments (mobile wallets) operated by some payments bank promoters are separate regulated entities, not subsidiaries of the bank.
• The credit-debit card distinction is a recurring UPSC trap: both look like 'cards' but debit is deposit-access and credit is loan-extension.

solution.concept_anchor: IPPB network size — 1.36 lakh post offices and 3 lakh postmen
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) pairing IPPB with '50,000 post offices' sounds plausible because students who broadly know IPPB uses the postal network without knowing the precise scale may accept a lower figure.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): IPPB is not operated under the Ministry of Finance — it operates under the Department of Posts which falls under the Ministry of Communications.

Confirm (b): IPPB operates through a network of over 1.36 lakh post offices, using more than 3 lakh postmen as banking agents — this correctly describes IPPB's delivery architecture and is the defining feature of its last-mile model.
Eliminate (c): IPPB is not solely for government employees — it serves the general public, particularly rural and underserved populations. This is a fabricated restriction.
Eliminate (d): The 50,000 post offices figure vastly understates IPPB's actual network of 1.36 lakh post offices — a significant geographic-swap distortion.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap in option (d) replaces the precise figure of 1.36 lakh post offices with 50,000 — a number large enough to seem plausible without being correct. Students who know IPPB uses the postal network but have not memorised the specific scale will find 50,000 acceptable. Similarly, option (a)'s ministry attribution (Finance vs. Communications) is a common institutional confusion for government-linked banks.
solution.final_explanation:
India Post Payments Bank's distinguishing feature is its unparalleled physical network — a key fact for examinations.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: IPPB operates under the Department of Posts, which falls under the Ministry of Communications (not Finance). The Ministry of Finance oversees the Finance Ministry's banking policy but does not administer IPPB directly.
• Option (b) — Correct: IPPB leverages a network of over 1.36 lakh post offices across India, with more than 3 lakh Grameen Dak Sewaks and postmen serving as banking agents equipped with micro-ATMs and smartphones. This is the largest physical banking delivery network in the country.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: IPPB is not restricted to government employees. It serves the general public — specifically targeting rural households, migrant workers, and beneficiaries of government schemes.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 50,000 post offices figure represents approximately one-third of IPPB's actual network. The correct figure is 1.36 lakh post offices.

Value Addition:
• The post office network's ubiquity in rural India — even in areas with no commercial bank branches — gives IPPB a structural advantage unmatched by private payments banks.
• IPPB's doorstep banking model directly supports DBT delivery for schemes like MGNREGS, PM-KISAN, and social security pensions.
• IPPB is the only payments bank with 100% government ownership, making it a public sector payments bank by design.

solution.concept_anchor: Payments Bank profitability challenge — no NIM plus high tech costs
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes — most payments banks have struggled to achieve consistent profitability due to the absence of NIM and high technology infrastructure costs. This is a documented challenge across the sector.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? Partially — the 75% SLR requirement is a real constraint, but R says it is the 'sole' reason for profitability challenges. The absence of NIM (from the no-lending rule) and high operating costs are equally or more significant. R overstates by using 'sole' — making it factually inaccurate as an absolute claim.
Step 3: A is correct; R is incorrect due to the overstated scope — option (c).
Confirm: Final step names option (c), matching correct_option.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap targets the word 'sole' in the Reason. It is true that the 75% SLR requirement constrains investment flexibility and limits return potential. But calling it the 'sole' reason for profitability challenges ignores the even more fundamental absence of NIM (no lending) and the substantial operating costs of running technology infrastructure. Students who read R quickly and accept the 75% SLR as a genuine constraint (which it is) may not notice the 'sole' qualifier that makes the Reason false as an absolute claim.
solution.final_explanation:
The profitability challenge of payments banks has multiple causal factors — reducing it to one is an analytical error.

Assertion (A): Correct. Profitability has been a persistent challenge for most payments banks. The combination of no NIM income, high technology infrastructure costs, and thin transaction fees has made sustainable profitability elusive. Several original licensees surrendered licenses partly due to commercial unviability.

Reason (R): Incorrect. While the 75% SLR requirement does constrain investment returns (sovereign securities yield less than commercial lending), it is not the 'sole' reason for profitability challenges. The primary structural constraint is the prohibition on lending — which removes NIM entirely. Additionally, high operating costs (technology platforms, compliance, agent networks) further strain margins. The word 'sole' makes the Reason factually wrong.

Since A is correct and R is incorrect, option (c) applies.

Value Addition:
• Among the original 11 licensees, only Airtel Payments Bank, Fino Payments Bank, IPPB, and Jio Payments Bank are currently operational and broadly viable.
• Fino Payments Bank turned profitable and listed on stock exchanges — an exception to the general trend.
• The payments bank model's viability may improve with volume-driven fee income growth as UPI transaction volumes continue to rise.

solution.concept_anchor: Payments Banks numerical parameters — capital, SLR, CRAR, promoter lock-in

statement_analysis.statement: The minimum paid-up equity capital for a payments bank at the time of licensing is Rs. 100 crore.
statement_analysis.reason: RBI's guidelines prescribe Rs. 100 crore as the minimum paid-up equity capital for a new payments bank — half the minimum required for a Small Finance Bank.

statement_analysis.statement: Payments banks must invest a minimum of 75% of their demand deposit balances in SLR-eligible government securities and treasury bills with maturity up to one year.
statement_analysis.reason: The 75% SLR investment requirement with a one-year maturity cap is a foundational prudential norm for payments banks under RBI guidelines.

statement_analysis.statement: The minimum Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) for payments banks is 12%, which is higher than the norm for scheduled commercial banks.
statement_analysis.reason: The minimum CRAR for payments banks is 15%, not 12%. The 12% figure does not correspond to any standard payments bank regulatory threshold.

statement_analysis.statement: A promoter of a payments bank must maintain a minimum equity holding of 40% for the first five years of the bank's operation.
statement_analysis.reason: The 40% promoter lock-in for five years is explicitly stipulated in RBI's payments bank licensing guidelines to ensure sustained promoter commitment during the establishment phase.

solution.strong_distractor: b — 'Only two' is a strong distractor for students who incorrectly validate Statement 3 by accepting 12% as close enough to 15% (both are 'above commercial bank norms'), or who doubt one of the other correctly stated parameters.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Rs. 100 crore minimum capital — correctly stated — Correct.
Statement 2: 75% SLR with one-year maturity cap — correctly stated — Correct.
Statement 3: 12% CRAR — incorrect; the correct figure is 15% — Incorrect.
Statement 4: 40% promoter lock-in for five years — correctly stated — Correct.
Three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct — select option (a): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3's entity-swap trap substitutes 12% for the correct 15% CRAR. The trap is designed to be ambiguous because 12% is a real figure in banking regulation — it is approximately the Tier 1 CRAR target for well-capitalised banks under Basel III in some contexts. Students who have seen 12% in banking regulation reading but have not specifically memorised the 15% payments bank figure will accept Statement 3 as 'in the right range.' The precise figure — 15% — is the only correct answer.
solution.final_explanation:
Precise numerical recall is essential when multiple regulatory parameters are tested simultaneously.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Rs. 100 crore minimum paid-up equity capital is the entry threshold for payments bank licensing. Small Finance Banks require Rs. 200 crore — twice this amount.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 75% demand deposit SLR investment rule with a one-year maturity ceiling is the central investment constraint that makes payments banks inherently low-risk institutions.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The minimum CRAR for payments banks is 15%, not 12%. The error is a deliberate substitution — 12% does not correspond to any standard payments bank prudential threshold. Commercial banks face a minimum of approximately 10.875% under Basel III-aligned RBI norms.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The 40% promoter equity lock-in for five years ensures skin-in-the-game accountability during the critical formative period of the institution.

Value Addition:
